681: A is correct because a customer managed KMS key can encrypt the EBS volumes and gives the company full control over key rotation, including enabling automatic annual rotation or triggering on-demand rotation whenever they choose. AWS managed keys rotate automatically but the company cannot control that rotation, and AWS owned keys offer no visibility or control at all. External key material adds unnecessary operational complexity for imported keys. A customer managed key satisfies the encryption-at-rest requirement with AWS KMS while retaining rotation control with the least operational overhead.
682: A is correct because an IAM policy that only permits creation of encrypted EBS volumes prevents new noncompliant resources at the source. AWS Config continuously evaluates EBS volumes against the encrypted-volumes rule to automatically identify noncompliant resources, and AWS Systems Manager automates remediation of the findings without manual intervention. Macie discovers sensitive data in S3, not EBS encryption, and Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities, so neither can detect unencrypted EBS volumes. This combination meets the detection and enforcement requirements with the least administrative overhead.
683: A is correct because migrating the web tier to EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer preserves the existing compute-based architecture, minimizing application changes, while adding self-healing and capacity elasticity across Availability Zones for resiliency. C is correct because migrating the single-node MySQL database to an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployment keeps the same MySQL engine with minimal application changes, and RDS automatically fails over to a standby in another Availability Zone to improve resiliency. The remaining options require significant rewrites, such as serverless Lambda or DynamoDB, or use a load balancer in a way that does not suit a stateful database.
684: B is correct because AWS Local Zones place compute and storage in metropolitan areas near the parent Region, and the company's VPC can be extended from eu-central-1 into the chosen Local Zone so applications run close to users with single-digit millisecond latency while remaining outside the Region itself to satisfy the regulatory restriction. CloudFront edge locations and regional edge caches only cache content and cannot host the application. Wavelength Zones target 5G mobile device workloads rather than general applications. Local Zones meet both the latency and the compliance requirements.
685: B is correct because Amazon RDS Proxy pools and shares database connections, keeping the number of open connections to the RDS for PostgreSQL instance predictable and preventing many concurrent Lambda invocations from overloading the database. The Lambda functions must be deployed inside the VPC to reach the RDS Proxy endpoint and the private DB instance over the network. RDS custom endpoints are an Aurora feature and do not provide connection pooling. Running the functions outside the VPC would not allow access to the private database.
686: C is correct because a transit gateway acts as a central network hub to which every VPC and on-premises location connects through a simple VPC or VPN attachment instead of many point-to-point links. As the number of accounts and VPCs grows, each new connection is just another attachment to the same hub, which simplifies administration and scales far better than full-mesh peering or a self-managed VPN instance. Direct Connect to a central VPC still requires peering for every new VPC and takes significant time to provision.
687: A is correct because deploying an Amazon SageMaker model and creating a SageMaker endpoint provides a fully managed, scalable real-time inference service, so the company receives predictions without managing any infrastructure. B is correct because Amazon SageMaker is a managed service that handles the training process, letting the company train a model on the historical data in the S3 bucket without needing in-house machine learning experience. Together these two steps cover both the training and the prediction requirements using managed services only.
688: C is correct because IAM Identity Center centralizes users across all accounts in the organization, and permission sets let permissions be managed at the group level. Permission sets that bundle the appropriate IAM policies are created for the developer and administrator groups and assigned to the groups across the accounts, so team permissions are consistent and centrally controlled. When new users are hired on either team, they are simply added to the appropriate group and immediately inherit the correct access, minimizing operational overhead. Assigning policies or permission sets to individual users, as in the other options, does not scale as teams grow.
689: D is correct because AWS Config provides a managed rule that automatically and continuously evaluates whether each EBS volume is encrypted and flags any unencrypted volume as noncompliant. This requires no custom code, scheduling, or compute infrastructure, minimizing both cost and configuration effort compared with writing and running API calls from Lambda or Fargate. Tag-based IAM policies and Cost Explorer do not verify encryption. AWS Config is the purpose-built, low-cost service for this kind of compliance check.
690: C is correct because S3 multipart uploads split a large file into parts that are transferred in parallel, driving much higher network throughput when uploading GB-sized files from on-premises to S3. D is correct because fetching multiple byte ranges of an object in parallel lets the EC2 instances download different portions of the object concurrently, maximizing download throughput from S3. These are both documented S3 performance recommendations for increasing transfer throughput. Random prefixes and additional buckets do not improve per-file transfer throughput.
691: B is correct because Amazon EFS is a shared, highly available file system that can be mounted concurrently by EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones and provides strong consistency, so frequent content changes are immediately visible to all instances. E is correct because S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency, and setting the Cache-Control metadata to no-cache ensures clients always retrieve the latest content, while CloudFront delivers it globally with low latency. EBS volumes cannot be attached across multiple instances in different Availability Zones, and DataSync is a migration tool rather than shared web storage.
692: A is correct because a Route 53 latency routing policy measures the latency between each user and each Region and automatically routes requests to the Region that provides the fastest response, which directly optimizes performance across the three Regions hosting the Application Load Balancers. Geolocation routing is based on user location rather than measured performance, and failover or geoproximity policies do not optimize for the lowest response time. An A record with a latency policy is the standard design for the most high-performing multi-Region experience.
693: D is correct because modifying the Auto Scaling group to span three Availability Zones makes the application highly available, and migrating the embedded NoSQL database to Amazon DynamoDB by using AWS DMS provides a fully managed, natively eventually consistent database. DynamoDB removes the operational burden of running and replicating the embedded database on EC2 instances, delivering the least operational overhead. The other options keep the database management burden on the company's own instances.
694: B is correct because Amazon ElastiCache for Redis caches catalog data from DynamoDB so reads are served from memory with the lowest possible latency, and Redis replication keeps that cache highly available. Storing shopping cart and session data in ElastiCache ensures the data persists independently of any individual server, so a user's cart survives disconnects and reconnects even as traffic scales. Sticky sessions tie users to single instances, OpenSearch is a search service rather than a low-latency session store, and a single EC2 instance with EBS is a single point of failure.
695: B is correct because Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights collects metrics, logs, and performance data from the EKS clusters and pods, giving visibility into cluster and container health. AWS X-Ray traces requests as they travel between the microservices, exposing latency, errors, and dependencies so performance issues can be pinpointed. Together they provide the observability the company needs for the microservices-based application. CloudTrail records API activity, Trusted Advisor provides best-practice checks, and ElastiCache improves performance but does not make the application observable.
696: C is correct because provisioning a separate KMS key for each customer and encrypting that customer's data server-side with SSE-KMS ties every customer's data to its own key. KMS key policies control which principals can use a key for decryption, so denying decryption to all principals except the IAM role that the customer provides ensures each customer can decrypt only their own data and company employees cannot decrypt it. An S3 bucket policy cannot reliably restrict KMS decryption operations, and ACM certificates secure TLS transport, not data encryption at rest.
697: B is correct because an internet-facing Application Load Balancer in the public subnets can receive inbound internet traffic on ports 80 and 443 and forward it to the EC2 instance registered as a target in the private subnet, with the DNS record pointing to the ALB. This keeps the instance in a private subnet per the security mandate while still making the web server reachable, since private subnets have no direct inbound internet path and a NAT gateway only provides outbound connectivity. The ALB serves as the secure public entry point for the application.
698: B is correct because Amazon EFS is a fully managed, highly available, and fault-tolerant shared file system that spans Availability Zones and can be mounted simultaneously by many containers through a StorageClass, including on AWS Fargate. EBS volumes are bound to a single Availability Zone and cannot be reliably shared across all containers, EBS Multi-Attach has significant limitations and is not supported for Fargate, and synchronizing multiple file systems with Lambda adds unnecessary overhead. EFS meets the persistence, sharing, and fault-tolerance requirements with the least operational overhead.
699: B is correct because Amazon ECS with the AWS Fargate launch type runs containers on fully managed serverless infrastructure, so the company manages no servers. Amazon EFS is a fully managed shared file system that can be mounted into Fargate tasks as persistent storage, replacing the on-premises host volume while requiring no storage infrastructure management. The EC2 launch types still require managing hosts, and an S3 bucket cannot be mounted as a standard persistent volume for containers.
700: A is correct because Network Load Balancers operate at Layer 4 and natively support both TCP and UDP traffic at high scale with low latency, and Global Accelerator supports internal NLBs as regional endpoints, so the application front end handles both protocols. C is correct because AWS Global Accelerator uses static anycast IP addresses on the AWS global edge network to route each user to the closest healthy Region, providing high availability through automatic failover and minimum latency for global users. CloudFront cannot proxy arbitrary TCP and UDP protocols, and DNS-based routing policies are slower and less reliable than anycast routing for this workload.
